subject: maths

moments.title: Fermat's marginal note
moments.body:
Fermat, a French lawyer and amateur mathematician, scribbles in the margin of his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica: 'It is impossible to separate a cube into two cubes, or a fourth power into two fourth powers, or in general, any power higher than the second, into two like powers. I have discovered a truly marvellous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain.'

The statement: there are no positive-integer solutions to a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for n greater than 2.

Fermat's son finds the note after Fermat's death (1665) and publishes it. The 'truly marvellous proof' is never found.
moments.takeaway: A 358-year mathematical puzzle is launched by a margin note that quite probably contained no real proof.

moments.title: Centuries of partial progress
moments.who: Many — Euler, Sophie Germain, Kummer, Faltings
moments.body:
Euler (1770) proves the case n = 3. Sophie Germain (early 1800s) shows the case n = 5 (with a critical refinement by Legendre). Dirichlet handles n = 14. Kummer's introduction of ideals (1840s) handles many primes.

Faltings's Theorem (1983) shows there are at most finitely many solutions for any n above 2. But 'finitely many' is not 'none' — the theorem doesn't close the question.

Progress is real but the full result remains elusive for 350 years.
moments.takeaway: Many of the most important developments in modern number theory came from attempts to prove Fermat's Last Theorem.

moments.title: Frey, Ribet — the link to modularity
moments.body:
Frey proposes that any non-trivial solution to Fermat's equation would give rise to an unusual elliptic curve (the 'Frey curve'). Ribet proves that such a curve cannot be modular — that is, cannot correspond to a modular form.

The Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture (proposed 1955) said ALL elliptic curves over the rationals are modular. If true, Fermat's Last Theorem follows immediately: no Frey curve can exist, so no solution can exist.
moments.takeaway: Fermat's Last Theorem reduces to a deep, central conjecture of modern number theory.

moments.title: Wiles works in secret, then in public
moments.body:
Wiles, who had been fascinated by Fermat since age 10, hears of Ribet's result and decides to attack Taniyama-Shimura for the class of curves Fermat needed.

He works in his attic for 7 years in near-total secrecy, telling almost no one. On 23 June 1993, at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge, he gives three lectures ending with a proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

A referee finds a gap in the proof in autumn 1993. Wiles spends another year — with help from Richard Taylor — repairing it. The complete proof is published in 1995.

quote.attrib: Andrew Wiles, at the end of his 1993 Cambridge lecture

moments.takeaway: Seven years of secret work, then a year of public crisis, then triumph. Fermat's Last Theorem is proved.

now.title: Fermat's legacy
now.body:
Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem also proved most of the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture for elliptic curves over the rationals. The full conjecture (modularity theorem) was completed by Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor in 2001.

Modern number theory builds on the techniques Wiles developed. Wiles received a Special Silver Plaque from the IMU and a 2016 Abel Prize.
now.open_questions: Can Wiles's methods be extended to other famous open problems? (Sato-Tate has been proved using similar methods.) Did Fermat have any kind of proof? (Almost certainly not — he never repeated the claim and his methods could only have handled n = 4, which he did publish.) What classical-sounding problems are still open in number theory?

reflection: Fermat probably did not have a proof. His margin note may have been a mistake or wishful thinking. Yet that mistake drove 350 years of mathematics, including some of the most important developments in the field. How much of mathematical progress is driven by problems that turn out to have been ill-posed or based on errors?
